question: What should a data warehouse achieve for the business, what components make it up, and why must the queryable presentation area be dimensional (fact and dimension tables) rather than normalized?

Fact table and dimension table vocabulary and the star join
Five myths about dimensional modeling and a top-10 list of pitfalls

limits: Opinionated practitioner guidance; no measurements, benchmarks or case data behind the percentages.
Text carries a 2002-era frame (ODS, OLAP cubes, relational DBMS optimiser claims, 'at the time of this writing'); cloud columnar warehouses, ELT and lakehouses are not covered.
Says normalized staging is acceptable but discouraged; later chapters (not in this file) handle grain types, bus matrix and slowly changing dimensions.
The 'enterprise data warehouse' is defined as the union of staging and presentation, which differs from the normalized-EDW usage of other schools.
practices: Design for business users first: understandable, consistent, adaptive, secure, decision-supporting, and accepted (p2-4, Goals).
If two measures have the same name they must mean the same thing; if they differ, label them differently (p3).
Keep the staging area off-limits to business users; any database that serves queries is part of the presentation area (p8-9).
A normalized staging database is acceptable but not the end goal; do not spend the budget on it before the dimensional presentation area exists (p9, Pitfall 7).
Present data in dimensional schemas (star schemas on a relational DBMS, cubes on OLAP) (p13).
Keep detailed atomic data in the presentation area; add aggregates only as performance helpers, never as a replacement (p12, Myth 1, Pitfall 3).
Build all data marts from conformed dimensions and facts on the bus architecture so marts can be combined (p12, Myth 5).
Organise data marts around business processes (orders, invoices, service calls), not departments; extract once from source (p25, Myth 2).
Store numeric additive measurements as facts at one grain per fact table; put textual descriptors in dimensions (p17-18).
Omit fact rows where nothing happened rather than loading zeros (p18).
Use a subset of the foreign keys as the composite primary key; do not add a ROWID key unless the DBMS requires it (p19).
Make dimension attributes verbose real words, replace or supplement codes with decoded text, and split intelligent codes into separate attributes (p20-21).

Decide fact versus attribute by whether the numeric field varies widely and participates in calculations (fact) or is a stable descriptor used in constraints (attribute); either is acceptable when unclear (p20).
Denormalise hierarchies (product, brand, category) into the dimension instead of snowflaking (p21).
Extend models in place: add dimensions with one value per existing fact row, add facts at the same grain, add attributes, via ALTER TABLE without reloading (p23).
Treat metadata as a planned deliverable with a repository, not an afterthought (p14-15).
Deliver an operational data store, if one is needed, as a hot partition of the warehouse rather than a third system (p16).
Serve most users through prebuilt parameterised applications rather than ad hoc tools (p14).
Handle updates to marts as managed loads, not transactional updates, and publish notice of dimension changes and new assumptions (p10, p13).

terms.definition: the primary table in a dimensional model where the numerical performance measurements of the business are stored
the list of dimensions at the intersection of which a measurement is taken; it tells us what the scope of the measurement is
Semiadditive facts can be added only along some of the dimensions, and nonadditive facts simply can't be added at all
integral companion to a fact table containing the textual descriptors of the business
the starlike structure of a fact table joined to a set of dimension tables
storing only a code (e.g. brand) in the dimension and creating a separate lookup table for it
the fact table's primary key made up of a subset of its foreign keys
all keys in the fact table match their respective primary keys in the dimension tables
a wedge of the overall presentation area pie; in its simplest form it presents the data from a single business process
common dimensions and facts shared by all data marts; the basis of the data warehouse bus architecture
detailed, unaggregated data in the presentation area required to withstand unpredictable ad hoc queries
both a storage area and a set of processes commonly referred to as extract-transformation-load (ETL); everything between the source systems and the presentation area
where data is organized, stored, and made available for direct querying by users, report writers, and other analytical applications
3NF / ER model: a design technique that seeks to remove data redundancies, dividing data into many discrete entities each a table
the union of all the diverse data warehouse components (staging and presentation), not just the normalized backroom
all the information in the data warehouse environment that is not the actual data itself
frequently updated, somewhat integrated copies of operational data, for operational reporting or real-time interactions
